newsitem.title: USA: US cattle prices seen struggling after USDA report.
newsitem.headline: US cattle prices seen struggling after USDA report.

text.p: CME cattle futures are expected to take little direction on Monday from Friday's U.S. Cattle-on-Feed report, but cash and futures prices will struggle going into the summer after the report's large on-feed number, livestock analysts said Friday.

"We have a lot of numbers to work through in the coming months and, even though (the report) was close to trade expectations, we carried some cattle over and that's a little negative," said Karl Skold, director of research for Frontier Risk Management.

The closly watched seven-state portion of the report showed May 1 on-feed supplies at 109 percent of a year ago, compared with the average trade estimate of 109.6 percent. Placements onto feed in April were reported at 112 percent versus the average estimate of 113.9 percent, and April marketings were 102 percent versus the average estimate of 101 percent.

Early trade indications were for June CME live cattle futures to open steady to 0.200 cent higher Monday, but analysts later said they expect futures to trade 0.200 cent on either side of Friday's close.
"What you are going to have to determine next week is where the cash is going to be and what you want your basis to be between cash and futures," said Jim Clarkson, analyst for A and A Inc.
But most analysts look for futures prices to trend lower along with cash markets as supplies of fed cattle loom large into the summer and early fall, they said.
Skold noted that the on-feed number for seven-state feedlots of 1,000 head or more was the highest since the start of the current reporting series.

"As we get into June, we are going to see more (fed) numbers and weights seasonally move up, and I think we are going to have lower prices as we go into the summer. Probably prices should go down to the low $60's," Skold said.

The May 1 on-feed number at 8.484 million head was 2.3 percent above the five-year average, 9.4 percent above last year's 7.758 million head and higher than the May 1995 number on-feed of 8.233 million head.

Andy Gottschalk, LFG senior vice president and livestock analyst, said that although most trade sources construed the marketings figure of 102 percent of last year as neutral to slightly bullish, he considered it bearish.
"The seasonal highs are in and we are going to work lower into the summer and early fall," Gottschalk said.
"It is the first of a series of sharply higher placements which will occur this quarter and which will lead to a backlog of fed cattle in the late summer and fall period," Gottschalk said.
